title: The Duchess of Malfi
author: John Webster
setting: Malfi (Amalfi), Rome, the shrine at Loretto, Ancona and Milan, in the early sixteenth century
lengthNote: Five acts, the longest of them the fourth; the Duchess is dead before the fifth begins
openingLine: You are welcome to your country, dear Antonio;
summary: A widowed duchess marries her steward in secret, against two brothers who have told her not to marry at all, and keeps the marriage hidden through three children while a hired spy reads her body for evidence. When it is found out, the brothers do not simply kill her: they build her a private theatre of dead hands, wax corpses and madmen first. Webster then gives the fifth act to the men who did it, and lets the murder finish them by accident, in the dark.
referenceStyle: act and scene — the text carries no line numbers, so quotations are placed by scene

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Duchess of Malfi
sourceText.note: The text follows the 1623 quarto with modernised spelling and no line numbering, so references stop at the scene. The horoscope Bosola reads in Act 2, Scene 3 dates the action to 1504.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: After The White Devil; the King's Men played it at the Blackfriars and the Globe, with Richard Burbage as Ferdinand.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: Nicholas Okes printed the quarto for John Waterson, with a cast list naming the original actors — a rarity for the period.

atAGlance.label: Source
atAGlance.note: William Painter's 1567 translation of Bandello's tale of Giovanna d'Aragona, Duchess of Amalfi, who really did marry her steward and vanish.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Years pass between Acts 2 and 3; the heroine dies in Act 4 and the last act belongs to her killers.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: The Duchess chooses
structure.summary: Antonio comes home from France praising a court kept clean at the top, and the play spends its first act showing the opposite. Ferdinand and the Cardinal hire Bosola to watch their sister and order her not to remarry; she waits until they have left the room and proposes to her steward, with Cariola behind the arras to witness a contract the church can only echo.

scenes.title: The fountain
scenes.summary: Antonio's account of the French court; Bosola, back from the galleys, is snubbed by the Cardinal.

scenes.title: The presence chamber
scenes.summary: Antonio describes the brothers; Ferdinand buys Bosola with gold and the provisorship of the horse.

scenes.title: The wooing
scenes.summary: The brothers' warning, the father's poniard, the will, the ring, and a marriage per verba de presenti.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: Bosola reads the body
structure.summary: Bosola has noticed that the Duchess is sick in the mornings and wearing a loose gown, and buys apricots to test her. She eats them greedily, goes into labour, and Antonio locks the court in its rooms on the pretext of a theft. Bosola finds the child's horoscope dropped in the courtyard and sends it to Rome, where Ferdinand reads it and starts imagining his sister in bed.

scenes.title: Apricots
scenes.summary: Bosola's meditation on the rotten body; the fruit ripened in horse-dung; the Duchess taken ill.

scenes.title: The gates shut
scenes.summary: A rumour of a Switzer with a pistol; Cariola brings news of a son.

scenes.title: The dark lantern
scenes.summary: Bosola and Antonio meet at night; Antonio's nose bleeds; the nativity is found.

scenes.title: Rome
scenes.summary: The Cardinal with his mistress Julia; Delio arrives with news that the letter has reached Ferdinand.

scenes.title: The mandrake
scenes.summary: Ferdinand's rage; the Cardinal, colder, waits to learn the father's name.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Confidence becomes betrayal
structure.summary: Years have passed and there are three children. Ferdinand enters the Duchess's bedchamber with a false key while she is talking to a husband who has slipped out, hands her his father's dagger and leaves without learning the man's name. She sends Antonio away under cover of a faked dismissal and then, moved by Bosola's praise of him, tells Bosola everything. The family is banished from Ancona in a dumb-show at Loretto, and Bosola returns in a visor to arrest her.

scenes.title: The false key
scenes.summary: Antonio and Delio count the years; Ferdinand dismisses the rumours to her face and plans to break in.

scenes.title: The bedchamber
scenes.summary: Marital teasing, then Ferdinand in the mirror; the poniard; the noble lie; Bosola told the truth.

scenes.title: The Cardinal turns soldier
scenes.summary: Rome prepares for war; the brothers learn of the pilgrimage and move to have her banished.

scenes.title: Loretto
scenes.summary: The Cardinal exchanges his robes for arms and strips the wedding ring from his sister's finger, in dumb-show.

scenes.title: The parting
scenes.summary: The Duchess's dream of pearls, the salmon and the dogfish, and Antonio sent to Milan with the eldest son.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Power becomes theatre
structure.summary: Ferdinand visits his sister in the dark, gives her a dead man's hand to kiss, and shows her the corpses of her husband and children, which are wax. He sends madmen to sing outside her door. Bosola comes disguised as a tomb-maker and a bellman, and she is strangled on stage after telling him she is Duchess of Malfi still. Cariola and the children follow. Ferdinand looks at the body and cannot bear it; Bosola asks for his wages and is given a pardon.

scenes.title: The dead hand
scenes.summary: Darkness, the hand, the wax figures, and the Duchess cursing the stars.

scenes.title: The madmen and the cord
scenes.summary: The masque of madmen, the tomb-maker's meditation on flesh, the dirge, the strangling, and Ferdinand's dazzled eyes.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Revenge misses its mark
structure.summary: In Milan Ferdinand has become a wolf in his own mind and digs up graves at night. The Cardinal tells Julia the secret and kills her with a poisoned Bible; Bosola overhears and turns. An echo from the Duchess's grave warns Antonio not to go to the Cardinal, and he goes, and Bosola kills him in the dark thinking he is someone else. The Cardinal's guests have promised not to answer his cries for help, and keep their word.

scenes.title: Antonio's lands
scenes.summary: Pescara gives Antonio's confiscated citadel to the Cardinal's mistress, and explains why.

scenes.title: Lycanthropy
scenes.summary: The doctor's diagnosis; Ferdinand attacks his shadow; Julia woos Bosola, extracts the secret from the Cardinal, and dies for it.

scenes.title: The echo
scenes.summary: Among the ruins of an abbey, Antonio hears his wife's voice tell him he will never see her more.

scenes.title: The wrong man
scenes.summary: Bosola stabs Antonio by mistake and tells him his family is dead.

scenes.title: The fishpond
scenes.summary: The Cardinal sees a thing with a rake; Bosola kills him; Ferdinand kills Bosola; Delio brings on the surviving son.

characters.name: The Duchess
characters.role: Widowed ruler of Malfi, sister to Ferdinand and the Cardinal
characters.summary: She is never given a first name, and answers to her title when everything else has been taken away. She proposes, she lies well when she must, she jokes with her husband about grey hair, and she meets a strangling with a lecture on the doors of death. Webster keeps her fear visible — she is full of daggers, she curses the stars — so that her composure at the end is earned rather than assumed.
characters.clue: She puts a wedding ring on her steward's finger to cure his eyesight, and is later handed a dead man's hand wearing a ring in the dark.

relationships.label: twin sister of, and murdered by
watched by, confides in, killed by

characters.name: Antonio Bologna
characters.role: Steward of the Duchess's household, then her husband
characters.summary: An honest man in a play that has no use for one. He opens the play with a theory of good government, wins at the ring, and is chosen by a woman who has to do all the choosing. Once the marriage is known he is reduced to a fugitive with a pistol and a good friend, and Webster kills him in the dark, by the wrong hand, at the moment he has decided to stop hiding.
characters.clue: He is told his master is making her will, is asked to be overseer, and finds himself kneeling with a ring on before he understands the conversation.

relationships.label: suspects, and is killed by mistake by

characters.name: Daniel de Bosola
characters.role: Ex-galley slave, intelligencer, provisor of the horse, murderer
characters.summary: He sees through everyone, including himself, and does the work anyway. He calls himself Ferdinand's creature in Act 1, reads the Duchess's pregnancy off her appetite in Act 2, is told the secret in Act 3 and sells it, and in Act 4 disguises himself twice to prepare her for death and then finds he cannot bear having done it. His revenge in Act 5 kills the one man he wanted to save.
characters.clue: He buys apricots to test a woman's condition, arrives at her prison as a tomb-maker and then a bellman, and asks for his wages over her body.

characters.name: Ferdinand
characters.role: Duke of Calabria, the Duchess's twin
characters.summary: He forbids his sister to remarry and will not say why, and the play lets the audience work it out from his imagery: her blood, her bed, the bargeman he pictures her with. His punishments are all designed to be looked at in the dark. When the body is in front of him he says the play's most famous line, blames Bosola, and within an act believes himself a wolf with the hair on the inside.
characters.clue: He hands his sister their father's dagger, later gives her a dead man's hand in the dark, and ends up digging in churchyards with a leg over his shoulder.

characters.name: The Cardinal
characters.role: The Duchess's elder brother, a churchman turned soldier
characters.summary: Ferdinand rages; the Cardinal arranges. He keeps a mistress, bribed his way towards the papacy, exchanges his robes for armour at a shrine, and kills Julia by making her kiss a poisoned book. He makes sure the guilt for the murder appears to belong to his brother, and dies asking to be laid by and never thought of.
characters.clue: He swears a woman to secrecy on a Bible he has poisoned, and arranges for nobody to answer when he calls for help.

relationships.label: slights, hires, and is killed by

characters.name: Cariola
characters.summary: She witnesses the marriage from behind the arras and closes the first act by wondering whether greatness or womanhood reigns most in her mistress. She is the practical voice — she dislikes the feigned pilgrimage — and at the end she is the one who fights, bites, scratches, claims a contract and a pregnancy, and is strangled anyway. Webster puts her death beside the Duchess's so that neither way of dying looks like the only one.
characters.clue: Hidden behind a hanging, she watches a wedding with no priest, and years later refuses to die quietly in the room next door to her mistress.

characters.name: Julia
characters.role: Castruccio's wife and the Cardinal's mistress
characters.summary: The court's other woman who chooses for herself, and the play's comment on what that looks like without a title. She takes lovers, pursues Bosola with a pistol, and is killed for wanting to know a secret. Her death by a kissed Bible is the Cardinal's cruelty in miniature: religion used as the instrument.
characters.clue: She holds a pistol on a man to make him confess to giving her a love-potion, and dies kissing a book.

characters.name: Delio
characters.summary: The confidant who survives. He is told the marriage first, keeps it, brings Julia money out of his own allowance, and is the one Antonio names with his last breath. His closing speech on integrity of life is the play's only attempt at consolation, and it is spoken over five bodies.
characters.clue: He walks in the ruins with a friend and points out the echo, and at the end he walks in with a boy.

themes.name: Marriage as a private act
themes.summary: The Duchess's marriage has no priest, no witnesses but Cariola, and no public existence, and it is legal. The play tests that private contract against the brothers' idea of marriage as a matter of blood and property: Ferdinand talks of the royal blood of Aragon and Castile, the Cardinal counts the dowry, and the Duchess asks what the church can force more. Her defence is that she has created no new world or custom, which is true and does not save her.
themes.development: Contracted in 1.3, evidenced by a pregnancy in Act 2, confessed in 3.2, and reduced in 4.2 to a ring on a dead hand.

themes.name: Secrecy and surveillance
themes.summary: Everyone is watching somebody. Bosola is paid to observe the Duchess; the Cardinal observes Bosola; Ferdinand enters a bedroom with a false key. The Duchess keeps her marriage secret for years and then gives it away in a moment of gratitude to the one man paid to find it. Webster's court is a place where a dropped piece of paper is evidence and a loose gown is a confession.
themes.development: The arras in 1.3, the dark lantern in 2.3, the false key in 3.1, the dumb-show in 3.4, and the servants who will not answer a cry for help in 5.5.

themes.name: Service and its price
themes.summary: Antonio is a steward, Bosola is a provisor of the horse, and both serve a great family that treats service as ownership. Bosola's complaint in Act 1 is that his service in the galleys went unpaid; his tragedy is that he goes on serving after he knows what it costs. Antonio's dying wish is that his son should fly the courts of princes.
themes.development: Bosola's hospital-beds speech in 1.1, his 'I am your creature' in 1.2, his demand for wages in 4.2, and Antonio's last instruction in 5.4.

themes.name: Identity under pressure
themes.summary: The play strips its heroine of her household, her husband, her children, her light and her hope, and then asks who she is. The answer — 'I am Duchess of Malfi still' — has been read as triumph and as delusion, and the scene supports both. Bosola meanwhile changes shape twice in Act 4 and admits that his own face is forfeited; Ferdinand ends up throttling his shadow.
themes.development: 'Whether the spirit of greatness or of woman' in 1.3; 'I am not mad yet' and the title claimed in 4.2; Ferdinand's wolf-skin in 5.2.

themes.name: Reputation
themes.summary: Ferdinand tells a fable in which Reputation, once parted from, is never found again. The play does not believe him: the Duchess's fame survives her, Delio's last speech is about it, and it is the brothers who leave no more print than a body fallen in snow. What the play does show is how reputation is manufactured — a strumpet by rumour, a Jew and a hermaphrodite by the officers who wanted Antonio's job.
themes.development: The brothers' warning in 1.3, the common rabble in 3.1, Ferdinand's fable in 3.2, and Delio on integrity of life in 5.5.

themes.name: Madness, real and performed
themes.summary: Ferdinand sends a consort of madmen to drive his sister mad and she tells Cariola that noise is the one thing keeping her sane. The madness that does arrive is his own: lycanthropia, the belief that he is a wolf, diagnosed by a doctor who proposes to beat it out of him. Webster puts the real disorder in the persecutor and lets the victim keep her wits to the last line.
themes.development: Cariola calls the marriage 'a fearful madness' in 1.3; the madmen dance in 4.2; Ferdinand digs up a leg in 5.2 and fights his own shadow.

techniques.name: Sententiae
techniques.definition: Rhymed moral maxims, usually a couplet, placed at the end of a speech or scene to sum it up as a general truth.
techniques.inThisBook: Almost every exit in the play carries one — 'Integrity of life is fame's best friend' — and the play's habit of moralising the action it has just shown is also how its characters excuse themselves.

techniques.name: Stage property
techniques.definition: An object handled on stage that carries far more weight than its use in the scene explains.
techniques.inThisBook: The wedding ring passes from the Duchess to Antonio to a severed hand; the poniard, the apricots, the horoscope and the poisoned Bible each do a scene's work on their own.

techniques.name: Dumb-show
techniques.definition: Action performed in mime, usually to music, while the dialogue stops.
techniques.inThisBook: The Cardinal's investiture as a soldier and the family's banishment at Loretto are played without words, watched by two pilgrims who supply the commentary the ceremony withholds.

techniques.name: The echo scene
techniques.definition: A device in which an echo returns the ends of a speaker's sentences as answers, apparently from the dead.
techniques.inThisBook: Among the ruins in 5.3 the echo speaks in the Duchess's voice, and its warnings — 'Do not', 'Never see her more' — are accurate and ignored.

techniques.name: Animal imagery
techniques.definition: Language that reduces people to beasts, appetite or prey.
techniques.inThisBook: Ferdinand calls his sister's children cubs and young wolves and ends believing he is a wolf himself; the Duchess is a caged robin, a pheasant fattened for the table, a salmon met by a dogfish.

techniques.name: Prose against verse
techniques.definition: Shifting between metrical speech and prose to mark status, sanity or intimacy.
techniques.inThisBook: Bosola drops into prose for his meditations on painted faces and rotten flesh and rises to verse for grief; Ferdinand's madness is in prose and his death-couplet in verse.

techniques.name: Dramatic irony
techniques.definition: The audience knows something a character on stage does not.
techniques.inThisBook: The Duchess praises Bosola for defending Antonio and rewards him with the secret; Antonio walks towards the Cardinal's chamber having been told by an echo not to; the Cardinal's guests keep their promise.

quotations.text: a prince’s court Is like a common fountain, whence should flow Pure silver drops in general, but if’t chance Some curs’d example poison’t near the head, Death and diseases through the whole land spread.
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: Antonio, home from France, describing the French king's reform of his court to Delio.
quotations.analysis: The play states its political theory in its first speech and then spends five acts illustrating the second half of it. 'Near the head' locates the poison exactly: the brothers, not the court, are the source. Antonio's own fate is the proof — the honest steward is the downstream casualty of what is poured in at the top.

quotations.text: places in the court are but like beds in the hospital, where this man’s head lies at that man’s foot, and so lower and lower.
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: Bosola, refused by the Cardinal, to Antonio and Delio.
quotations.analysis: His image is a ward, not a ladder: nobody climbs, everyone lies down, and the arrangement runs only one way. The prose is deliberate — Bosola's bitterest observations are unmetrical, as if verse were a courtesy he no longer extends. It also predicts his own place in the play, which is always at somebody's foot.

quotations.text: Say, then, my corruption Grew out of horse-dung: I am your creature.
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: Accepting the provisorship of the horse, and Ferdinand's gold, in exchange for spying on the Duchess.
quotations.analysis: He names the bribe for what it is, in the coarsest terms available, and takes it in the same sentence. 'Creature' meant a dependant made by a patron, and Bosola uses it with the full sense of having been manufactured; the word comes back on him in Act 4 when Ferdinand disowns what he made. The horse-dung will also ripen the apricots.

quotations.text: Such weddings may more properly be said To be executed than celebrated.
quotations.speaker: Ferdinand
quotations.context: The brothers warning their sister against a private marriage, in a speech she says sounds rehearsed.
quotations.analysis: A pun that is also a plan. 'Executed' is the legal word for completing a contract, and the Duchess will shortly use exactly that language for her own wedding; it is also the other word, and Ferdinand means both. The Duchess's reply — that the speech between them 'was studied' — notices that her brothers are performing, which is what the whole family will do to her later.

quotations.text: This was my father’s poniard, do you see? I’d be loth to see’t look rusty, ’cause ’twas his.
quotations.speaker: Ferdinand
quotations.context: Ferdinand, alone with his sister after the Cardinal has left, before calling her a lusty widow.
quotations.analysis: The dagger is introduced as an heirloom and a threat in the same breath, and 'rusty' is the euphemism for unused. He will put it into her hand in 3.2 and she will show it to Antonio, who notices it has a handle as well as a point. It is the play's first stage property, and the family's authority is in it: the father's blade, the brother's grip.

quotations.text: The misery of us that are born great! We are forc’d to woo, because none dare woo us;
quotations.speaker: The Duchess
quotations.context: To Antonio, who has understood what she is doing and is afraid to answer.
quotations.analysis: Rank has inverted the courtship, and she says so as a complaint about greatness rather than a boast. The lines that follow compare her to a tyrant who 'fearfully equivocates', which is a strange self-description for a woman proposing marriage: she knows that speaking in riddles is what power does, and that she is having to do it. It is the last time in the play she will be the one with power.

quotations.text: This is flesh and blood, sir; ’Tis not the figure cut in alabaster Kneels at my husband’s tomb. Awake, awake, man!
quotations.speaker: The Duchess
quotations.context: Antonio is trembling; she tells him what she is.
quotations.analysis: She refuses the role of the kneeling effigy on a husband's monument, which is the widowhood her brothers want. The play remembers the image: in 4.2 Cariola tells her she looks like her picture in the gallery, and Bosola describes tomb-effigies that no longer pray. Webster lets her insist on flesh and blood and then shows what the court does to flesh and blood.

quotations.text: We now are man and wife, and ’tis the church That must but echo this.
quotations.speaker: The Duchess
quotations.context: After the two of them have knelt and exchanged vows, with Cariola as witness.
quotations.analysis: A spousal per verba de presenti was binding in canon law, and the Duchess knows it — she has 'heard lawyers say' so. What is striking is the verb: the church is reduced to an echo, and the play's own echo in 5.3 will speak from her grave. The marriage that needed no ceremony is the one thing in the play nobody can annul.

quotations.text: Whether the spirit of greatness or of woman Reign most in her, I know not; but it shows A fearful madness. I owe her much of pity.
quotations.speaker: Cariola
quotations.context: Cariola alone, closing the first act after the couple have gone in.
quotations.analysis: The witness to the marriage refuses to bless it. Her pair of alternatives — greatness or woman — assumes the two are different spirits, which is the assumption the Duchess has just defied, and 'madness' is the word Ferdinand will later try to make literal. Giving the act's last word to the servant rather than the lovers is Webster's way of keeping the audience from settling.

quotations.text: I have this night digg’d up a mandrake.
quotations.speaker: Ferdinand
quotations.context: Ferdinand's first words on entering with Bosola's letter about the birth.
quotations.analysis: The mandrake root was said to shriek when pulled up and to drive the hearer mad, so the sentence announces the letter's effect before its contents. 'Digg'd up' also puts Ferdinand in a churchyard at night, which is where the doctor will find him in Act 5 with a leg over his shoulder. His madness is planted here, three acts before it is diagnosed.

quotations.text: Why might not I marry? I have not gone about in this to create Any new world or custom.
quotations.speaker: The Duchess
quotations.context: To Ferdinand, who has broken into her bedchamber and told her to cut out her own tongue.
quotations.analysis: The question is genuine and unanswered, because Ferdinand's objection is not a reason. Her defence is conservatism — she has invented nothing — and the play agrees with her: widows remarried, stewards were gentlemen, the law recognised the contract. What she has done is exercise a freedom that everybody else in the play assumes belongs to men.

quotations.text: You have shook hands with Reputation, And made him invisible. So, fare you well: I will never see you more.
quotations.speaker: Ferdinand
quotations.context: The end of his fable of Reputation, Love and Death, who parted and took three ways.
quotations.analysis: The fable says reputation is lost once and for ever, and it is told by a man who will spend two acts making sure. 'I will never see you more' is a vow he keeps in the letter and breaks in the spirit — he sees her in the dark, unseen, with a dead man's hand. Webster's fables are always spoken by the character least entitled to their morals.

quotations.text: Why should only I, Of all the other princes of the world, Be cas’d up, like a holy relic? I have youth And a little beauty.
quotations.speaker: The Duchess
quotations.context: Her last words to Ferdinand before he leaves the bedchamber.
quotations.analysis: 'Cas'd up' is the language of the reliquary, a body preserved and displayed, and it is exactly the fate her brothers have in mind for her: the alabaster figure of Act 1 in another form. 'A little beauty' is the plainest thing anybody says about themselves in the play. Ferdinand's answer is that some virgins are witches, which is not an answer.

quotations.text: A politician is the devil’s quilted anvil; He fashions all sins on him, and the blows Are never heard:
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: Alone, having just been told the secret of the marriage by the Duchess herself.
quotations.analysis: The anvil is padded so that the hammering makes no noise, and Bosola has just demonstrated the technique on the woman who thanked him for it. What follows is a complaint about the base quality of intelligencer and then the decision to inform anyway; the soliloquy is the play's clearest case of a man describing his own corruption accurately and proceeding. 'Never heard' is what the court depends on.

quotations.text: The birds that live i’ th’ field On the wild benefit of nature live Happier than we; for they may choose their mates, And carol their sweet pleasures to the spring.
quotations.speaker: The Duchess
quotations.context: Banished from Ancona, with her train shrunk to a few servants, moments before Bosola arrives with the letter.
quotations.analysis: Choosing a mate is the one thing she has done and the one thing the birds are allowed. The image is picked up in her prison, where she tells Cariola that the robin-redbreast and the nightingale never live long in cages, and by Bosola, who compares the soul to a lark in a cage. Webster's birds are always either free or dead.

quotations.text: I account this world a tedious theatre, For I do play a part in’t ’gainst my will.
quotations.speaker: The Duchess
quotations.context: After the dead hand and the wax figures, when Bosola offers to save her life.
quotations.analysis: She has just been made the audience for a show her brother designed, and she describes her situation as being cast. The metaphor is literal here in a way it is not in Shakespeare's versions of it: there are artificial figures behind a curtain, a masque of madmen is coming, and the man talking to her will shortly change costume twice. 'Tedious' is the unexpected word — not terrible, but long.

quotations.text: I am Duchess of Malfi still.
quotations.speaker: The Duchess
quotations.context: To Bosola, disguised as a tomb-maker, who has asked whether she is not some great woman.
quotations.analysis: Six words, and the play's title inside them. Bosola's reply — that this is what makes her sleep so broken — is not a rebuttal but a diagnosis, and productions can play the line as defiance, as delusion, or as a plain statement of fact by someone who has stopped arguing. What she claims is not her name, which the play never gives, but her office, which her brothers cannot take.

quotations.text: Thou art a box of wormseed, at best but a salvatory of green mummy. What’s this flesh? a little crudded milk, fantastical puff-paste.
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: Bosola as tomb-maker, answering the Duchess's question 'Who am I?'
quotations.analysis: The Duchess asks for her identity and is given an inventory of her ingredients. The vocabulary is the apothecary's — wormseed was a drug, mummy a medicine made from corpses — so the body is already being priced as material. Bosola's prose here is the same instrument he used on the painted Old Lady in Act 2; the play's contempt for flesh is his idiom, and he is now applying it as a kindness.

quotations.text: Hark, now everything is still, The screech-owl and the whistler shrill Call upon our dame aloud, And bid her quickly don her shroud!
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: The bellman's dirge, sung to the Duchess after the executioners have entered with a coffin, cords and a bell.
quotations.analysis: The bellman went round London's prisons the night before an execution ringing and reciting, so the Duchess is being given a public ritual in a private room. The tetrameter couplets are the madmen's metre from earlier in the scene, calmed down: Webster moves from howling to lullaby without changing the beat. 'Our dame' is the only affectionate thing Bosola calls her, and it comes in a song about her death.

quotations.text: What would it pleasure me to have my throat cut With diamonds? or to be smothered With cassia? or to be shot to death with pearls? I know death hath ten thousand several doors For men to take their exits;
quotations.speaker: The Duchess
quotations.context: Bosola has suggested that the cord should terrify her.
quotations.analysis: She refuses to be frightened by the instrument, and does it by listing luxurious alternatives that are still deaths. The diamonds and pearls are her coronet from the dream in 3.5, in which the diamonds turned to pearls and Antonio read them as tears. 'Exits' is a stage word, and she goes on to say the doors open both ways — the one certainty she claims is that she is leaving.

quotations.text: heaven-gates are not so highly arch’d As princes’ palaces; they that enter there Must go upon their knees.
quotations.speaker: The Duchess
quotations.context: Her reason for kneeling before the executioners pull.
quotations.analysis: A stage direction disguised as theology: she kneels, and gives the audience a reason that turns the posture of submission into one of entry. The comparison with princes' palaces is her last word on her own rank — heaven is lower-built than Malfi, and she has to stoop to get in. It is also the humbler version of Antonio's roof in 1.3, which she said was too low to stand upright in.

quotations.text: The death Of young wolves is never to be pitied.
quotations.speaker: Ferdinand
quotations.context: Bosola has shown him the strangled children.
quotations.analysis: He called them cubs in the previous scene, and the animal language has hardened from insult to sentence: wolves may be killed without pity by definition. The word comes back within an act when Ferdinand is diagnosed with lycanthropia and says he is a wolf with the skin inside. Webster lets the imagery convict its user.

quotations.text: Cover her face; mine eyes dazzle: she died young.
quotations.speaker: Ferdinand
quotations.context: Looking at his sister's body, after Bosola asks whether he will weep.
quotations.analysis: Three clauses, an order, a symptom and an epitaph, and no connective between them. The man who insisted on darkness for his visits cannot bear to look now that there is light, and 'dazzle' is the eye failing rather than the heart breaking. Bosola's dry answer — that her infelicity seemed to have years too many — refuses the sentiment, and Ferdinand's next move is to blame the executioner.

quotations.text: Mine! was I her judge? Did any ceremonial form of law Doom her to not-being?
quotations.speaker: Ferdinand
quotations.context: Bosola has said the murder was done by Ferdinand's authority.
quotations.analysis: The tyrant discovers due process at the moment it would inconvenience him. The questions are unanswerable in the way he wants because the answer is yes, he was, and the play has shown the whole trial: the false key, the dead hand, the madmen. 'Not-being' is an extraordinary coinage for a man who cannot say 'death' about what he has ordered.

quotations.text: Said he was a wolf, only the difference Was, a wolf’s skin was hairy on the outside, His on the inside; bade them take their swords, Rip up his flesh, and try.
quotations.speaker: Doctor
quotations.context: The doctor describing Ferdinand's lycanthropia to Pescara.
quotations.analysis: The diagnosis is reported, not shown, and the reporting makes it clinical: a disease with a name and a case history. Ferdinand's own account of himself is the play's most exact — the wolf was always on the inside — and his invitation to cut him open and check is the same demand for evidence that Bosola made of the Duchess's body. What the brothers did to her flesh, he now asks to have done to his.

quotations.text: My duchess is asleep now, And her little ones, I hope sweetly. O heaven, Shall I never see her more?
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: Among the ruins of an abbey by the Cardinal's window, where an echo answers from the Duchess's grave.
quotations.analysis: The echo replies 'Never see her more', and it is the only repetition Antonio says he marked. He still thinks she is asleep; the audience has watched her strangled an act ago, so the echo is telling the truth to the one person who cannot hear it as truth. The scene is built out of a stage trick and works as grief because the dead are answering with the living man's own words.

quotations.text: We are merely the stars’ tennis-balls, struck and banded Which way please them.
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: Having stabbed Antonio in the dark, and recognised him by his voice.
quotations.analysis: The man who planned every move in the play discovers accident at the moment his plan kills the wrong person, and reaches for fate. Tennis was a court game, played indoors, with balls that went where they were hit; the image keeps the killing in the palace. Bosola's own last account of Antonio's death — 'in a mist; I know not how' — is the same idea with the metaphor gone.

quotations.text: In all our quest of greatness, Like wanton boys whose pastime is their care, We follow after bubbles blown in th’ air.
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: Antonio dying, having been told that his wife and children are dead.
quotations.analysis: His last generalisation is about greatness, which he never sought, and the couplet is the kind of sententia the play hands to everybody; it is odd and moving that the one honest man gets a commonplace to die on. The instruction that follows it is more particular: let my son fly the courts of princes. Delio's final speech will do the opposite and set the boy up in his mother's right.

quotations.text: When I look into the fishponds in my garden, Methinks I see a thing arm’d with a rake, That seems to strike at me.
quotations.speaker: The Cardinal
quotations.context: Alone with a book on hell, before Bosola comes in with Antonio's body.
quotations.analysis: The Cardinal's conscience arrives as a reflection in still water, which is the fountain image from the play's first speech gone stagnant. The 'thing arm'd with a rake' is a devil out of a doom-painting, and he sees it in his own garden, at the bottom of his own pond. It is the closest the coldest character comes to feeling anything, and he dismisses it with 'lay him by' about the book.

quotations.text: Whether we fall by ambition, blood, or lust, Like diamonds, we are cut with our own dust.
quotations.speaker: Ferdinand
quotations.context: Ferdinand's dying words, having remembered his sister.
quotations.analysis: Diamond can only be cut with diamond dust, so the couplet says that great men are destroyed by their own substance — and Ferdinand, who has just wounded his brother and killed Bosola in the same scuffle, is the example. The Duchess called diamonds precious for having passed through many hands in 1.3, and Ferdinand answered that whores by that rule are precious. The image has been waiting five acts to be turned on him.

quotations.text: In a mist; I know not how: Such a mistake as I have often seen In a play.
quotations.speaker: Bosola
quotations.context: Malatesti has asked how Antonio came by his death.
quotations.analysis: Bosola's answer confesses the killing and calls it a theatrical convention in the same breath, which is either the play excusing its own plotting or the most honest thing in it: mistaken identity in the dark is what tragedies do, and he has been in one. The Duchess called the world a tedious theatre in Act 4; Bosola, dying, agrees with her about the genre.

quotations.text: Integrity of life is fame’s best friend, Which nobly, beyond death, shall crown the end.
quotations.speaker: Delio
quotations.context: The last lines of the play, spoken with Antonio's son beside him and five bodies on the stage.
quotations.analysis: The closing sententia is the tidiest thing in a play that has refused to be tidy, and readers have long argued over whether Webster means it. The boy it is spoken over was given a horoscope in Act 2 promising a short life and a violent death, which the audience remembers and Delio does not mention. The consolation is offered; the play has already put a question mark after it.

timeline.label: Antonio Bologna murdered in Milan
timeline.detail: The historical steward-husband of Giovanna d'Aragona, Duchess of Amalfi, was killed some years after his wife and children had been seized and disappeared.

timeline.label: Bandello's Novelle published
timeline.detail: The Italian collection in which the Duchess's story first circulated in print, told by a writer who claimed acquaintance with Antonio.

timeline.label: Painter's Palace of Pleasure
timeline.detail: William Painter's English translation of the tale, Webster's direct source, with a moral firmly against the Duchess.

timeline.label: The White Devil printed
timeline.detail: Webster's first surviving tragedy, another Italian court story, published with a preface complaining about its reception at the Red Bull.

timeline.label: The Duchess of Malfi on stage by this year
timeline.detail: The King's Men performed it at the Blackfriars and the Globe; William Ostler, the original Antonio, died in December 1614.

timeline.label: The quarto printed
timeline.detail: Nicholas Okes for John Waterson, with commendatory verses and a list of the actors who first played the parts.

timeline.label: Peggy Ashcroft and John Gielgud at the Haymarket
timeline.detail: A wartime London revival with Ashcroft as the Duchess and Gielgud as Ferdinand that returned the play to the mainstream repertory.

timeline.label: The Sam Wanamaker Playhouse opens with the play
timeline.detail: The candlelit indoor theatre beside Shakespeare's Globe chose Webster's play for its first production, restoring the darkness the Blackfriars scenes were written for.

criticalViews.summary: The Duchess is the play's moral centre, a woman who chooses her husband, governs her household and faces death on her own terms, destroyed by brothers whose objection to her marriage is possession dressed as honour. On this reading the fifth act shows what is left when she is gone: men in the dark, killing each other by mistake.
criticalViews.counter: The play gives her a secret marriage, a noble lie and a feigned pilgrimage, and Cariola calls her choice a fearful madness. Webster's sympathy is not the same as approval.

criticalViews.summary: He is on stage more than anyone, he has the soliloquies, and the play's argument about service, conscience and the price of employment runs through him. The Duchess's death is his crisis rather than hers, and the fifth act is his revenge tragedy.
criticalViews.counter: A play with Bosola at the centre has to explain why its title, its most quoted line and its most carefully built scene all belong to somebody else.

criticalViews.position: Sensation and horror for their own sake
criticalViews.summary: An older complaint, still made: the dead hand, the wax corpses, the madmen and the lycanthropy are a showman's tricks, and Webster's genius is for the moment rather than the design. The fifth act, on this view, is a run of good lines in search of a structure.
criticalViews.counter: The horrors are all theatrical in the play's own terms — Ferdinand stages them and says so — and the fifth act's accidents are the argument that violence, once begun, cannot aim.

criticalViews.position: A play about the Jacobean court
criticalViews.summary: Read against the intelligencers, the patronage and the sexual politics of James's court, the play is a study of a system in which advancement is bought with information and a great family's honour is a matter of bloodlines. The Cardinal turning soldier and the Pope seizing a dukedom are politics, not melodrama.
criticalViews.counter: The political reading tends to flatten the twins into representatives, when Ferdinand's fixation on his sister is the least systematic thing in the play.

essayQuestions.question: 'I am Duchess of Malfi still.' How far is the Duchess's identity her own creation?
essayQuestions.focus: Identity, rank and the claims made on her body
plan: Start with the wooing in 1.3, where she rejects the alabaster figure and defines herself as flesh and blood.
Trace the brothers' counter-definitions: strumpet, holy relic, cub-bearer, and the body that Bosola reads for evidence in Act 2.
Examine 4.2, where her question 'Who am I?' is answered with wormseed and puff-paste, and she answers it herself with her title.
Weigh what the title is worth: she claims an office she no longer holds, in a prison, to a man in disguise.
Conclude on the play's refusal to give her a first name, and what that withholding does to the claim.

essayQuestions.question: How far is Bosola responsible for what he does?
plan: Set out his case in 1.1 and 1.2: unpaid service in the galleys, neglect, and a bribe he names as corruption while taking it.
Follow the intelligencer at work in Acts 2 and 3, and note how often he describes his own baseness accurately before acting.
Examine the turn in 4.2: the disguises, the dirge, the request for wages, and the grief that comes only after she is dead.
Consider the fifth act as revenge, and the accident that kills Antonio, which he blames on the stars.
Decide whether the play lets 'much 'gainst mine own good nature' stand, or whether his self-knowledge is the indictment.

essayQuestions.question: What is Act 5 for?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, revenge and the play after the Duchess
plan: State the problem: the heroine dies in Act 4 and the play continues for another act without her.
Read the fifth act as the consequences of the fourth — lycanthropy, the poisoned book, the echo, the mistaken killing.
Show how the act echoes earlier scenes: the Cardinal's fishpond and Antonio's fountain, Ferdinand's wolf and his young wolves.
Test the view that it is a run of horrors against the view that it demonstrates how violence, once begun, cannot aim.
Close on Delio's final couplet and the surviving son, and whether the ending consoles or merely stops.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the presentation of Ferdinand's relationship with his sister.
essayQuestions.focus: The twin, the poniard and the dark
plan: Begin with 1.3: the father's poniard, the 'lusty widow', and a prohibition with no reason given.
Read his imagery in 2.5 — the mandrake, the bargeman, the burning sheets — as evidence the play gives without stating a diagnosis.
Examine 3.2 and 4.1, in which he sees her only in the dark or unseen, and what that staging implies.
Consider the twin motif: 'I had liv'd her time to a minute', and the wolf-skin turned inward in Act 5.
Weigh the possible readings — dynastic pride, incestuous desire, madness — and argue for the one the text best supports without excluding the others.

discussionQuestions: The Duchess's marriage is legal and needs no priest. Why does the play make her hide it for years?
Bosola tells the truth about himself in nearly every soliloquy. Does that make him better or worse than the brothers?
Ferdinand never says why his sister must not remarry. What would the play lose if he did?
The Duchess dies in Act 4. What happens to the audience's attention in Act 5, and is that what Webster wanted?
The play ends with a couplet about integrity of life spoken over a boy whose horoscope predicted a violent death. Is the ending hopeful?

related.why: The earlier Renaissance tragedy of damnation: Marlowe's devils are theological, Webster's wear cardinals' robes.
Another paid intelligencer who reads a woman's body for evidence and destroys a marriage from inside the household.
Revenge tragedy with a malcontent at the centre, and the same question of what a good man does in a rotten court.
A contract marriage, a churchman's hypocrisy and a woman's body treated as the state's business, played as comedy.
Written a few years earlier: the other Jacobean tragedy that lets the worst happen in the fourth act and goes on.
